text: Il visitatore entra e dice: "Quanti libri! Li ha letti tutti?" All'inizio ritenevo che la frase rivelasse solo persone di scarsa dimestichezza con il libro, aduse a vedere solo scaffaletti con cinque gialli e una enciclopedia dei ragazzi a dispense. Ma l'esperienza mi ha insegnato che la frase viene pronunciata anche da persone insospettabili. Si può dire che si tratta pur sempre di persone che hanno una nozione dello scaffale come deposito di libri letti e non della biblioteca come strumento di lavoro, ma non basta. Ritengo che di fronte a molti libri chiunque sia preso dall'angoscia della conoscenza, e fatalmente scivoli verso la domanda che esprime il suo tormento e i suoi rimorsi.
translation: The visitor comes in and says: "So many books! Have you read them all?" At first I thought the remark betrayed only people with little familiarity with books, used to seeing small shelves holding five detective novels and a children's encyclopaedia in instalments. But experience has taught me that the remark is uttered even by people above suspicion. One can say that they are still people who think of the shelf as a store of books already read and not of the library as a working tool, but that is not enough. I believe that in front of many books anyone is seized by the anguish of knowledge, and fatally slides towards the question that expresses his torment and his remorse.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, 'Come giustificare una biblioteca privata', in Il secondo diario minimo (Milano: Bompiani, 1992) [first published as a 'Bustina di Minerva', L'Espresso, 1990]
notes: Opening of the library section of the essay; establishes the library as 'strumento di lavoro' (working tool) rather than a deposit of read books.

text: Io un tempo avevo adottato la risposta sprezzante: "Non ne ho letto nessuno, altrimenti perché li terrei qui?" Ma è una risposta pericolosa perché scatena l'ovvia reazione: "E dove mette quelli che ha letto?" Migliore è la risposta standard di Roberto Leydi: "Molti di più, signore, molti di più", che gela l'avversario e lo piomba in uno stato di stuporosa venerazione. Ma la trovo impietosa e ansiogena. Ora ho ripiegato verso l'affermazione: "No, questi sono quelli che debbo leggere entro il mese prossimo, gli altri li tengo all'università", risposta che da un lato suggerisce una sublime strategia ergonomica, e dall'altro induce il visitatore ad anticipare il momento del congedo.
translation: I once adopted the contemptuous answer: "I haven't read any of them, otherwise why would I keep them here?" But it is a dangerous answer because it triggers the obvious reaction: "And where do you put the ones you have read?" Better is Roberto Leydi's standard answer: "Many more, sir, many more", which freezes the adversary and plunges him into a state of stupefied veneration. But I find it merciless and anxiety-inducing. Now I have fallen back on the statement: "No, these are the ones I have to read by next month, the others I keep at the university", an answer that on the one hand suggests a sublime ergonomic strategy, and on the other induces the visitor to hasten the moment of leave-taking.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, 'Come giustificare una biblioteca privata', in Il secondo diario minimo (Milano: Bompiani, 1992) [first published as a 'Bustina di Minerva', L'Espresso, 1990]
notes: The canonical three answers. Roberto Leydi was an ethnomusicologist and friend of Eco.

text: In the past I adopted a tone of contemptuous sarcasm. 'I haven't read any of them; otherwise, why would I keep them here?' But this is a dangerous answer because it invites the obvious follow-up: 'And where do you put them after you've read them?' The best answer is the one always used by Roberto Leydi: 'And more, dear sir, many more,' which freezes the adversary and plunges him into a state of awed admiration. But I find it merciless and angst-generating. Now I have fallen back upon the riposte: 'No, these are the ones I have to read by the end of the month. I keep the others in my office,' a reply that on the one hand suggests a sublime ergonomic strategy, and on the other hand leads the visitor to hasten the moment of his departure.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, 'How to Justify a Private Library', in How to Travel with a Salmon & Other Essays, trans. William Weaver (San Diego: Harcourt, 1994), p. 117
url: http://logismoitouaaron.blogspot.com/2008/12/how-to-justify-private-library.html (blog reproducing the Weaver translation with page reference; archive.org copy howtotravelwiths00ecou is borrow-only)
notes: William Weaver's published English version of q02; 'by the end of the month' and 'in my office' differ slightly from the Italian ('entro il mese prossimo', 'all'università').

text: Naturalmente il bibliofilo, anche chi colleziona libri contemporanei, è esposto all'insidia dell'imbecille che ti entra in casa, vede tutti quegli scaffali, e pronuncia: "Quanti libri! Li ha letti tutti?" L'esperienza quotidiana ci dice che questa domanda viene fatta anche da persone dal quoziente intellettivo più che soddisfacente. Di fronte a questo oltraggio esistono, a mia scienza, tre risposte standard. La prima blocca il visitatore e interrompe ogni rapporto, ed è: "Non ne ho letto nessuno, altrimenti perché li terrei qui?" Essa però gratifica l'importuno solleticando il suo senso di superiorità e non vedo perché si debba rendergli questo favore. La seconda risposta piomba l'importuno in uno stato d'inferiorità, e suona: "Di più, signore, molti di più!" La terza è una variazione della seconda e la uso quando voglio che il visitatore cada in preda a doloroso stupore. "No," gli dico, "quelli che ho già letto li tengo all'università, questi sono quelli che debbo leggere entro la settimana prossima."
translation: Naturally the bibliophile, even one who collects contemporary books, is exposed to the snare of the imbecile who walks into your house, sees all those shelves, and pronounces: "So many books! Have you read them all?" Daily experience tells us that this question is asked even by people with a more than satisfactory IQ. Faced with this outrage there exist, to my knowledge, three standard answers. The first stops the visitor and cuts off all relations: "I haven't read any of them, otherwise why would I keep them here?" But it gratifies the intruder by tickling his sense of superiority and I don't see why we should do him that favour. The second plunges the intruder into a state of inferiority, and goes: "More, sir, many more!" The third is a variation on the second and I use it when I want the visitor to fall prey to painful astonishment. "No," I tell him, "the ones I have already read I keep at the university; these are the ones I have to read by next week."
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, lectio magistralis at the Fiera Internazionale del Libro di Torino, May 2007 (published as 'La memoria vegetale', in La memoria vegetale e altri scritti di bibliofilia, Rovello 2007 / Bompiani 2011)
url: https://www.libriantichionline.com/bibliofilia/umberto_eco_quanti_libri (reproduces the passage; source line: 'Lectio magistralis alla Fiera del Libro di Torino, 2007')
notes: Eco's later (2007) rewriting of the three answers; here the deadline is 'next week'. The same passage is voiced in Ferrario's 2022 film (see che-fare.com review).

text: Visto che la mia biblioteca conta cinquantamila volumi, l'infelice cerca soltanto di anticipare il momento del commiato, adducendo improvvisi impegni. Quello che l'infelice non sa è che la biblioteca non è solo il luogo della tua memoria, dove conservi quel che hai letto, ma il luogo della memoria universale, dove un giorno, nel momento fatale, potrai trovare quello che altri hanno letto prima di te. È un repositorio dove al limite tutto si confonde e genera una vertigine, un cocktail della memoria dotta.
translation: Since my library holds fifty thousand volumes, the unhappy man only tries to bring forward the moment of farewell, pleading sudden engagements. What the unhappy man does not know is that the library is not only the place of your memory, where you keep what you have read, but the place of universal memory, where one day, at the fatal moment, you will be able to find what others have read before you. It is a repository where, at the limit, everything blurs together and generates a vertigo, a cocktail of learned memory.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, lectio magistralis at the Fiera Internazionale del Libro di Torino, May 2007 (published as 'La memoria vegetale', in La memoria vegetale e altri scritti di bibliofilia, Rovello 2007 / Bompiani 2011)
url: https://www.libriantichionline.com/bibliofilia/umberto_eco_quanti_libri (reproduces the passage; source line: 'Lectio magistralis alla Fiera del Libro di Torino, 2007')
notes: Continuation of q04. Widely quoted in the 2026 Bologna coverage (zero.eu) together with 'Una biblioteca non è una somma di libri – è un organismo vivente con una vita autonoma'.

text: Una biblioteca non è una somma di libri – è un organismo vivente con una vita autonoma […] La biblioteca non è solo il luogo della tua memoria, dove conservi quel che hai letto, ma il luogo della memoria universale, un repositorio dove al limite tutto si confonde e genera una vertigine, un cocktail della memoria dotta.
translation: A library is not a sum of books – it is a living organism with a life of its own […] The library is not only the place of your memory, where you keep what you have read, but the place of universal memory, a repository where at the limit everything blurs together and generates a vertigo, a cocktail of learned memory.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, lectio magistralis at the Fiera Internazionale del Libro di Torino, May 2007 (published as 'La memoria vegetale', in La memoria vegetale e altri scritti di bibliofilia, Rovello 2007 / Bompiani 2011) — as quoted in Zero.eu, 'A Bologna apre la Biblioteca Eco: 32mila libri, nello stesso ordine in cui li aveva lasciati il professore', July 2026
notes: The 'organismo vivente' opening sentence could only be found in secondary quotation (Zero.eu, AIB Notizie); the second sentence matches q05 verbatim.

text: Una biblioteca di casa non è solo un luogo in cui si raccolgono libri: è anche un luogo che li legge per conto nostro.
translation: A home library is not only a place where books are gathered: it is also a place that reads them on our behalf.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, as quoted in Rivista Studio, 'Comprare libri per non leggerli' (6 February 2017)
notes: Rivista Studio quotes the sentence in these words from a lectio magistralis of Eco's; AIB Notizie attributes a variant ('Una biblioteca non si limita a raccogliere i tuoi libri, li legge anche per conto tuo') to a Bustina di Minerva in L'Espresso (1998); the underlying argument (you absorb unread books by handling, dusting and cross-reading) is in the essays of La memoria vegetale. Neither primary text has been read.

text: The writer Umberto Eco belongs to that small class of scholars who are encyclopedic, insightful, and nondull. He is the owner of a large personal library (containing thirty thousand books), and separates visitors into two categories: those who react with "Wow! Signore professore dottore Eco, what a library you have! How many of these books have you read?" and the others—a very small minority—who get the point that a private library is not an ego-boosting appendage but a research tool. Read books are far less valuable than unread ones. The library should contain as much of what you do not know as your financial means, mortgage rates, and the currently tight real-estate market allows you to put there. You will accumulate more knowledge and more books as you grow older, and the growing number of unread books on the shelves will look at you menacingly. Indeed, the more you know, the larger the rows of unread books. Let us call this collection of unread books an antilibrary.
speaker: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable (New York: Random House, 2007), Prologue / ch. 1 'Umberto Eco's Antilibrary, or How We Seek Validation'
notes: The passage that coined 'antilibrary'; Taleb's 'thirty thousand' refers to the Milan flat only.

text: There are several ways of responding to the person who comes to your house, notices your impressive library and can only think to ask, 'Have you read them all?' One of my friends used to say, 'And more, my dear sir, and more.' Personally, I've two replies. The first: 'No. These are just the books I'm planning to read next week. The ones I've already read are at the university.' The second: 'I haven't read any of these books. Why would I keep them, otherwise?'
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter 'All the books we haven't read'
notes: Eco's 2009 conversational retelling of the three answers.

text: There are more books in the world than hours in which to read them. And that doesn't just apply to all the books ever published, but even to only the most important books of a particular culture. We are thus deeply influenced by books that we haven't read, that we haven't had the time to read. Who has actually read Finnegans Wake — I mean from beginning to end? Who has read the Bible properly, from Genesis to the Apocalypse? If I were to combine all the sections I've read, I could boast of about one-third. But no more. And yet I've a fairly accurate notion of what I haven't read.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter 'All the books we haven't read'
notes: Eco on Pierre Bayard and the books one knows without having read them; he adds that he owns three editions of the Mahabharata in three languages and has never read it.

text: And now, to reply to your question, I only possess about thirty incunabula, though they do include what you might call the 'essentials'. For instance, the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, the Nuremberg Chronicle, Ficino's translation of the Corpus Hermeticum, the Arbor Vitae Crucifixae Jesu Christi by Ubertino Da Casale (who became one of the characters in my Name of the Rose), and so on. My collection is very focused. It is a Bibliotheca Semiologica Curiosa Lunatica Magica et Pneumatica, or 'a collection dedicated to the occult and mistaken sciences'. For example, I have Ptolemy, who was wrong about the movement of the Earth, but not Galileo, who was right.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter on incunabula ('Tell me about your collection')
notes: Eco's own gloss of the collection's name. The Braidense fund actually counts 36 incunabula (AIB Studi 2022).

text: Io ho solo una trentina di incunaboli ma ho certamente quelli di cui un collezionista non può fare a meno (gli incontournables, come va di moda dire oggi in Francia, quelli a cui non puoi girare intorno) […]. La mia collezione è molto orientata. Si tratta di una Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa lunatica magica et pneumatica, detto altrimenti di una collezione dedicata al sapere occulto e al sapere falso. Ho Tolomeo, che si sbagliava sul moto della Terra, ma non ho Galileo, che aveva ragione.
translation: I have only about thirty incunabula but I certainly have the ones a collector cannot do without (the incontournables, as it is fashionable to say in France today, the ones you cannot get around) […]. My collection is very focused. It is a Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa lunatica magica et pneumatica, in other words a collection devoted to occult knowledge and false knowledge. I have Ptolemy, who was wrong about the motion of the Earth, but not Galileo, who was right.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri (Milano: Bompiani, 2009), p. 112, as quoted in Angela Nuovo and Aldo Coletto, 'Gli incunaboli di Umberto Eco', AIB studi 62 (2022)
notes: Italian edition wording of q11; 'sapere occulto e sapere falso' is the phrase the Fondazione and Braidense reuse ('occult knowledge and false learning').

text: I have all his books except the Ars Magnesia, which is impossible to get hold of, despite being a small book with no illustrations. Kircher wasn't yet known at the time of publication, so I expect only a few copies were printed. Also, the book is so devoid of charm that probably no one thought it worth saving. But I also possess the works of Robert Fludd and a fair few other eccentric minds.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter on incunabula (answering Carrière on Athanasius Kircher)
notes: On Kircher and Fludd; Eco adds that collectors prize Kircher for 'the exceptional beauty of his books' and that he taught a 1992 course on Kircher's reading of hieroglyphs.

text: I am fascinated by error, by bad faith and idiocy. Like Flaubert. You and I both adore silliness. In Faith in Fakes I describe visiting American museums that show reproductions of art works, including a waxwork Venus de Milo with arms. In The Limits of Interpretation I create a theory of fakes and forgeries. With regard to my novels, Foucault's Pendulum was inspired by occultists who believe feverishly in everything, whereas the main character in Baudolino is a delightful and, in the end, benevolent charlatan.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009) (Carrière: 'And how do you explain this bizarre choice?')
notes: Why the collection is devoted to error and forgery.

text: My secretary once wanted to draw up a catalogue of my books so that she knew exactly where each one was. I persuaded her not to. While I was writing The Search for the Perfect Language I looked at my library anew, with new criteria, and changed it around. Which books would best nourish my thoughts on the subject? When I finished writing, some books went back on the linguistics shelf, and some to aesthetics, but others were already being used for a new piece of research.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter on organising a library
notes: Direct testimony that the shelves were re-sorted by research project; Carrière replies that 'if you classified by subject, you'd have books by someone like Kircher on every shelf'.

text: I think people often confuse a collection of books that one owns with a collection of ancient books. I have 50,000 books in my various homes. But these are modern books. I also have 1,200 rare titles. There's another difference, too. The ancient books are books I have chosen and paid for, whereas the modern ones are made up not only of the books I have bought over the years, but also, and increasingly, those that people have sent me as tributes. I give lots of them to my students, but I do keep a fair few, and that's how I've got to 50,000.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009) (de Tonnac: 'How large are your collections?')
notes: The 50,000 / 1,200 figures Eco himself used from about 2008 on.

text: I obviously wouldn't want my collection to be dispersed. My family could give it to a public library, or else sell it through an auction house, which would mean the collection would go to a university intact. That's all I care about.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter 'What will happen to your library after you die?'
notes: What actually happened: the rare books went to the state (Braidense, 2018/2021), the modern library on 90-year loan to Bologna (2026).

text: I don't know if mine is an accurate reflection of me. As I've said, I collect books whose contents I don't believe, so it must be more like a mirror image. Or perhaps a reflection of my contradictory nature. I'm not sure, because I don't show my collection to many people. A book collection is a solitary, masturbatory kind of phenomenon, and you don't often come across people who share your passions. If you own beautiful paintings, people come over to admire them. But no one is sincerely interested in your collection of old books.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009)
notes: Matches the family's account that only a few friends were admitted to the Stanza degli antichi.

text: Having spoken so passionately in favour of books, I had better admit that the first thing I would save is my 250-gigabyte hard drive, which contains all my writing from the last thirty years. After that, if there were still time, I would of course try to save one of my oldest books — not necessarily the most valuable, but the one I love the most. But how to choose? I am extremely attached to lots of them. I would hope not to have too long to deliberate. Perhaps I would take Bernhard von Breydenbach's Peregrinatio in Terram Sanctam, Spier, Drach, 1490, on account of its wonderful illustrated plates on several folded pages.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009) (Carrière: 'Your house is on fire — what would you save first?')
notes: The fire question. Elsewhere in the book: 'It's no accident that I wrote a book about a library burning down. I'm always worrying about it happening to my house' (the fire chief lived upstairs when he was a child).

text: I own a total of about fifty thousand books. But as a rare books collector I am fascinated by the human propensity for deviating thought. So I collect books about subjects in which I don't believe, like kabbalah, alchemy, magic, invented languages. Books that lie, albeit unwittingly. I have Ptolemy, not Galileo, because Galileo told the truth. I prefer lunatic science.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Lila Azam Zanganeh, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197', The Paris Review 185 (Summer 2008)
notes: Answer to 'Your library here in Milan is a legend in and of itself. What kind of books do you like to collect?'

text: I don't go to the bookshelves to choose a book to read. I go to the bookshelves to pick up a book I know I need in that moment. It's a different story. For instance, if you were to ask me about contemporary authors, I would look through my collections of Roth or DeLillo to remember exactly what I loved. I am a scholar. In a way I should say I am never freely choosing. I am following the needs of the job I am doing at any given time.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Lila Azam Zanganeh, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197', The Paris Review 185 (Summer 2008)
notes: Answer to 'With so many volumes, when you go to the bookshelf, how do you decide which book to pick up and read?'

text: I receive an enormous quantity of books every day—novels, new editions of books I already own—so every single week I fill up some boxes and send them off to my university, where there is a big table with a sign that says take a book and run.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Lila Azam Zanganeh, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197', The Paris Review 185 (Summer 2008)
notes: Answer to 'Do you ever give books away?'

text: The apartment is a labyrinth of corridors lined with bookcases that reach all the way up to extraordinarily high ceilings—thirty thousand volumes, said Eco, with another twenty thousand at his manor. I saw scientific treatises by Ptolemy and novels by Calvino, critical studies of Saussure and Joyce, entire sections devoted to medieval history and arcane manuscripts. The library feels alive, as many of the books seem worn from heavy use; Eco reads at great speed and has a prodigious memory. In his study, a maze of shelves contains Eco's own complete works in all their translations (Arabic, Finnish, Japanese . . . I lost count after more than thirty languages).
speaker: Lila Azam Zanganeh (interviewer)
source: Lila Azam Zanganeh, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197', The Paris Review 185 (Summer 2008)
notes: Eyewitness description, August 2007; the living room had 'several glass cases displaying seashells and rare comics, a lute, a collection of recorders' and the Castello Sforzesco visible through the windows. Research placement: 'corridoio / studio (bookcase Q for translations)'.

text: I'm afraid that, by now, it might actually be 50,000 books. When my secretary wanted to catalogue them, I asked her not to. My interests change constantly, and so does my library. By the way, if you constantly change your interests, your library will constantly be saying something different about you. Besides, even without a catalogue, I'm forced to remember my books. I have a hallway for literature that's 70 meters long. I walk through it several times a day, and I feel good when I do. Culture isn't knowing when Napoleon died. Culture means knowing how I can find out in two minutes.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die', SPIEGEL interview with Umberto Eco by Susanne Beyer and Lothar Gorris, Spiegel Online International, 11 November 2009
notes: Answer to 'you have a library of 30,000 volumes. It probably doesn't work without a list or catalogue.' Page fetched directly with curl (spiegel.de blocks WebFetch). Research placement: 'corridoio (bookcase A, literatures)'.

text: The list is the origin of culture. It's part of the history of art and literature. What does culture want? To make infinity comprehensible. It also wants to create order — not always, but often. And how, as a human being, does one face infinity? How does one attempt to grasp the incomprehensible? Through lists, through catalogs, through collections in museums and through encyclopedias and dictionaries.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die', SPIEGEL interview with Umberto Eco by Susanne Beyer and Lothar Gorris, Spiegel Online International, 11 November 2009
notes: Opening answer of the interview about the Louvre exhibition 'Vertige de la liste' (2009).

text: We have a limit, a very discouraging, humiliating limit: death. That's why we like all the things that we assume have no limits and, therefore, no end. It's a way of escaping thoughts about death. We like lists because we don't want to die.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die', SPIEGEL interview with Umberto Eco by Susanne Beyer and Lothar Gorris, Spiegel Online International, 11 November 2009
notes: The sentence that gave the interview its title.

text: The list doesn't destroy culture; it creates it. Wherever you look in cultural history, you will find lists. In fact, there is a dizzying array: lists of saints, armies and medicinal plants, or of treasures and book titles. Think of the nature collections of the 16th century. My novels, by the way, are full of lists.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die', SPIEGEL interview with Umberto Eco by Susanne Beyer and Lothar Gorris, Spiegel Online International, 11 November 2009
notes: 'Lists of book titles' and Wunderkammern: the same logic as his own catalogues and the mirabilia in the Stanza degli antichi.

text: We have three types of memory. The first one is organic, which is the memory made of flesh and blood and the one administrated by our brain. The second is mineral […] this second type is also the electronic memory of today's computers, based upon silicon. We have also known another kind of memory, the vegetal one, the one represented by the first papyruses […] and then on books, made of paper. […] Libraries, over the centuries, have been the most important way of keeping our collective wisdom. They were and still are a sort of universal brain where we can retrieve what we have forgotten and what we still do not know. If you will allow me to use such a metaphor, a library is the best possible imitation, by human beings, of a divine mind, where the whole universe is viewed and understood at the same time.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, 'Vegetal and Mineral Memory: The Future of Books', lecture delivered at the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, 1 November 2003 (published by the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, 2003; Italian version in La memoria vegetale)
notes: The 'vegetal memory' definition in Eco's own English; the lecture ends 'Long life to this temple of vegetal memory.'

text: uno dei malintesi che dominano la nozione di biblioteca è che si vada in biblioteca per cercare un libro di cui si conosce il titolo. In verità accade sovente di andare in biblioteca perché si vuole un libro di cui si conosce il titolo, ma la principale funzione della biblioteca, almeno la funzione della biblioteca di casa mia e di qualsiasi amico che possiamo andare a visitare, è di scoprire dei libri di cui non si sospettava l'esistenza, e che tuttavia si scoprono essere di estrema importanza per noi. Ora, è vero che questa scoperta può essere data sfogliando il catalogo, ma non c'è niente di più rivelativo e appassionante dell'esplorare degli scaffali che magari riuniscono tutti i libri di un certo argomento, cosa che intanto sul catalogo per autore non si sarebbe potuto scoprire, e trovare accanto al libro che si era andati a cercare un altro libro, che non si era andati a cercare, ma che si rivela come fondamentale. Cioè, la funzione ideale di una biblioteca è di essere un po' come la bancarella del bouquiniste, qualcosa in cui si fanno delle trouvailles, e questa funzione può essere permessa solo dalla libera accessibilità ai corridoi degli scaffali.
translation: One of the misunderstandings that dominate the notion of a library is that one goes to the library to look for a book whose title one knows. In truth it often happens that one goes to the library because one wants a book whose title one knows, but the main function of the library, at least the function of the library in my own house and of any friend's we may go to visit, is to discover books whose existence one did not suspect, and which nevertheless turn out to be of extreme importance to us. Now, it is true that this discovery can come from leafing through the catalogue, but there is nothing more revealing and exciting than exploring shelves that perhaps gather all the books on a certain subject, something one could not have discovered in the author catalogue, and finding next to the book one went looking for another book, which one had not gone looking for, but which turns out to be fundamental. That is, the ideal function of a library is to be a bit like the bouquiniste's stall, something in which one makes trouvailles, and this function can only be allowed by free access to the corridors of the shelves.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, De Bibliotheca, lecture given 10 March 1981 at Palazzo Sormani for the 25th anniversary of the Biblioteca Comunale di Milano (Milano: Biblioteca Comunale, 'I quaderni di Palazzo Sormani', 1981; repr. in Sette anni di desiderio, Bompiani 1983)
url: https://www.liberliber.eu/mediateca/libri/e/eco/de_bibliotheca/pdf/de_bib_p.pdf (Liber Liber e-text, 'per gentile concessione dell'Autore e della Bompiani')
notes: The source of the popular paraphrase 'a library is a place where you go to find books you didn't know you needed'; note 'la biblioteca di casa mia' and the subject-shelving argument that explains his own arrangement.

text: se la biblioteca è, come vuole Borges, un modello dell'Universo, cerchiamo di trasformarla in un universo a misura d'uomo, e, ricordo, a misura d'uomo vuol dire anche gaio, anche con la possibilità del cappuccino
translation: if the library is, as Borges would have it, a model of the Universe, let us try to turn it into a universe on a human scale, and, I recall, on a human scale also means cheerful, even with the possibility of a cappuccino
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, De Bibliotheca, lecture given 10 March 1981 at Palazzo Sormani for the 25th anniversary of the Biblioteca Comunale di Milano (Milano: Biblioteca Comunale, 'I quaderni di Palazzo Sormani', 1981; repr. in Sette anni di desiderio, Bompiani 1983)
url: https://www.liberliber.eu/mediateca/libri/e/eco/de_bibliotheca/pdf/de_bib_p.pdf (Liber Liber e-text, 'per gentile concessione dell'Autore e della Bompiani')
notes: Closing of the 1981 lecture, after the 21-point 'negative model' of the bad library.

text: La biblioteca è effettivamente simbolo e realtà di una memoria collettiva. Dante Alighieri, quando arriva nell'ultimo canto del Paradiso e ha la visione beatifica di Dio, com'è che descrive Dio, che non è una cosa facile? E dice: "vidi raccolto in un volume ciò che nell'universo si squaderna". Quindi vede Dio come la biblioteca delle biblioteche, con un po' di secoli in anticipo su Jorge Luis Borges.
translation: The library is truly the symbol and the reality of a collective memory. Dante Alighieri, when he reaches the last canto of Paradiso and has the beatific vision of God, how does he describe God, which is not an easy thing? He says: "I saw gathered in one volume what is scattered in leaves throughout the universe". So he sees God as the library of libraries, a few centuries ahead of Jorge Luis Borges.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:01:55)
notes: Opening of the film, over the long tracking shot of Eco walking his corridors (footage from 'Sulla memoria', 2015; same words at Hq66X9f-zgc 00:04:18). Auto-caption cleaned: 'horg e Luis' = Jorge Luis.

text: Qui siamo nello studio di mio padre, dentro la casa che lui e mia madre hanno scelto trent'anni fa per poter tenere tutta la collezione di libri di mio padre, cioè i 1200 libri antichi e i 30.000 libri moderni. Qui lui lavorava al computer, telefonava; c'era anche il posto di lavoro delle persone che collaboravano in casa. La stanza degli antichi invece era un po' il rifugio dove si chiudeva a suonare il flauto, comunque a guardare i libri antichi: non portava computer né telefoni.
translation: Here we are in my father's study, inside the house that he and my mother chose thirty years ago so as to be able to keep my father's whole book collection, that is the 1,200 old books and the 30,000 modern books. Here he worked at the computer, made phone calls; there was also the workplace of the people who worked with him at home. The room of the ancients, on the other hand, was rather the refuge where he shut himself away to play the flute, or anyway to look at the old books: he took neither computer nor telephones in there.
speaker: Carlotta Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:05:25)
notes: Carlotta Eco introducing the studio and the Stanza degli antichi; gives the 1,200 / 30,000 figures. Research placement: 'studio; antichi'.

text: Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa lunatica magica et pneumatica.
translation: Semiological, curious, lunatic, magical and pneumatic library.
speaker: voice-over reading Eco's bookplate / collection title
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:06:18)
notes: The collection's Latin name read aloud (auto-caption 'la Colle bas è biblioteca' = probably 'la collezione: Bibliotheca…'). The same title card is read at 00:00:21 of the trailer clips FeIUY9EhZgI and bcK8rOkcb3k, followed by 'Athanasius Kircher', 'Difetti e pregi dei Promessi Sposi', 'King Lear di William Shakespeare'.

text: fisionomica; magia; alchimia; chimica e scienze; teatri chimici; occultismo; ermetismo; magia; semiologia ed emblemi; geroglifici; scienze astronomiche; demonologia e alchimia; esoterismo; teologia; Kircher; Kircher; Rosa Croce; lingue universali; semiologia e linguistica; anima delle bestie
translation: physiognomy; magic; alchemy; chemistry and sciences; chemical theatres; occultism; hermeticism; magic; semiology and emblems; hieroglyphs; astronomical sciences; demonology and alchemy; esotericism; theology; Kircher; Kircher; Rosicrucians; universal languages; semiology and linguistics; the soul of beasts
speaker: voice-over reading the section labels of the Stanza degli antichi
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:07:00)
notes: The subject labels of Eco's rare-book shelves read out in sequence over shots of the Stanza degli antichi; they match the Braidense ECO.01–04 section order and the AIB Studi description. Speaker identity not confirmed on screen.

text: Questi papà non li usava mai. Beh, i libri vanno toccati, insomma, con le mani.
translation: These ones Dad never used. Well, books have to be touched, you know, with your hands.
speaker: Carlotta Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:07:40)
notes: Said while handling the old books (about gloves, apparently); consistent with Eco's 'toccare la carta che fa ancora crac crac sotto le dita' (Il Foglio 2022).

text: Una grande casa può dare l'impressione dell'umanista letterato che vive così appartato dal mondo. La casa è grande appunto perché i libri altrimenti non ci stanno: in quella precedente sono stato sfrattato con concorso del genio civile, perché pareva che le librerie facessero crollare i muri.
translation: A big house can give the impression of the literary humanist living cut off from the world. The house is big precisely because otherwise the books would not fit: from the previous one I was evicted with the help of the civil engineering office, because it seemed the bookcases would bring the walls down.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:08:40)
notes: Archival interview used in the film; the official English subtitles of the clip ygvl-_gtAP8 (00:00:44–00:01:02) render it 'The house is big otherwise I wouldn't know where to put the books. I was evicted from the last one after an inspection by the city engineers because they were afraid the floors would collapse.' Auto-caption 'collare' corrected to 'crollare'.

text: When I arrived 25 years ago they were 30.000… I have no more time to count them. […] They are my books, translations… and they are books on me.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Official English-subtitled clip of 'Umberto Eco: A Library of the World' (Ferrario 2022), subtitle times 00:01:22 and 00:01:38; same interview in the Louisiana Channel film (M8IWTOFNlOc, 00:22:49–00:24:10)
notes: Louisiana Channel version (Tonny Vorm, Milan, May 2015): 'All together in different places there should be about 50,000. Here, when I arrived 25 years ago there were 30,000 … I think there are 35,000.' Research placement: 'studio (bookcases M/Q: books by and about Eco)'.

text: La memoria vegetale, visto che i libri si fanno purtroppo ormai col legno, ma una volta anche però col papiro eccetera: la memoria vegetale è quella dei libri; la memoria organica è quella del nostro cervello; e poi c'è una memoria minerale che è quella del silicio, che è la memoria elettronica. Noi, nella misura in cui possiamo dire "io", siamo la nostra memoria, cioè la memoria è l'anima. C'è un corrispettivo della memoria individuale, che è la memoria vegetale della biblioteca: l'insieme delle biblioteche è l'insieme della memoria dell'umanità.
translation: Vegetal memory, since books are unfortunately now made of wood, but once also of papyrus and so on: vegetal memory is the memory of books; organic memory is that of our brain; and then there is a mineral memory, that of silicon, which is electronic memory. We, insofar as we can say "I", are our memory, that is, memory is the soul. There is a counterpart of individual memory, which is the vegetal memory of the library: the sum of all libraries is the sum of humanity's memory.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:09:36)
notes: Also in 'Sulla memoria' part 1 (Hq66X9f-zgc, 00:00:43 and 00:03:25) and in the subtitled clip ygvl-_gtAP8 ('Libraries are mankind's common memory').

text: Noi siamo esseri temporali, viviamo nel tempo: senza memoria non si costruisce, non si progetta il proprio futuro.
translation: We are temporal beings, we live in time: without memory one does not build, one does not plan one's own future.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:11:08)
notes: From the 2015 'Sulla memoria' material reused in the film (cf. zj1kwT87ne0 00:04:02–00:04:53: 'Senza memoria non c'è anima. Per proiettarci sul futuro bisogna avere un'anima').

text: Se papiri e manoscritti sono sopravvissuti per migliaia di anni e disponiamo di libri freschissimi stampati più di cinquecento anni fa, non sappiamo quanto sopravvivano i supporti elettronici. Non lo sappiamo, perché i nostri computer attuali non sono più in grado di leggere quanto avevamo registrato qualche decennio fa sui paleolitici floppy disc.
translation: If papyri and manuscripts have survived for thousands of years and we have perfectly fresh books printed more than five hundred years ago, we do not know how long electronic media will survive. We do not know, because our present computers are no longer able to read what we recorded a few decades ago on palaeolithic floppy disks.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:20:58)
notes: Eco text (from the 'Bustina di Minerva' / Carrière conversations) voiced in the film; also in the trailer clips (bcK8rOkcb3k 00:00:50).

text: Forse voi avete letto quella novella di Borges dove c'è un personaggio che si chiama Funes il memorioso, che ricorda tutto […] ha una memoria totale ed è praticamente un imbecille, perché non ce la fa. È come il web: se noi dovessimo di colpo sapere tutto quello che c'è nel web diventeremmo pazzi. Quindi qual è la seconda virtù della memoria? La prima è quella che conserva, la seconda è quella che filtra. Guai se la memoria, sia individuale che collettiva, non facesse delle decimazioni giorno per giorno, buttasse via quello che non vale la pena.
translation: Perhaps you have read that story by Borges with a character called Funes the Memorious, who remembers everything […] he has a total memory and is practically an imbecile, because he cannot cope. It is like the web: if we suddenly had to know everything that is on the web we would go mad. So what is the second virtue of memory? The first is the one that preserves, the second is the one that filters. Woe if memory, individual as well as collective, did not carry out decimations day by day, throwing away what is not worth keeping.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:22:51)
notes: Memory as selection; the library as a filtered memory rather than an archive of everything. Caption 'filica' read as 'filtra' (context).

text: Il nostro rischio è di una perdita di memoria per eccesso, ormai, di memoria artificiale. Schiaccio un bottone e mi arriva una bibliografia di diecimila titoli; con una bibliografia di diecimila titoli io non faccio niente, prendo la bibliografia e la butto via. Una volta andavo in biblioteca, trovavo tre libri, ma almeno tre libri li leggevo e riuscivo a dire qualcosa; adesso con diecimila non li leggo più. Allora ecco, vede, lì dove noi crediamo di avere conquistato una memoria immensa, l'abbiamo perduta.
translation: Our risk is a loss of memory through an excess, by now, of artificial memory. I press a button and a bibliography of ten thousand titles arrives; with a bibliography of ten thousand titles I do nothing, I take the bibliography and throw it away. Once I went to the library, I found three books, but at least I read those three books and managed to say something; now with ten thousand I no longer read them. So there, you see, where we believe we have conquered an immense memory, we have lost it.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:26:10)
notes: The same argument appears in the Bustina di Minerva of 2000 cited by AIB Notizie ('riceve una bibliografia di diecimila titoli, e rinuncia'). Final word 'persa' inferred from context (caption cuts at 'l'abbiamo').

text: Quel tanto di vita che si conquista leggendo non discrimina tra grandi opere d'arte e letteratura di trattenimento: non fatevi ricattare da chi vi dice che bisogna leggere solo i libri importanti. Ho ricordi intensi e bellissimi anche di libri forse sciocchi, ma che mi hanno nutrito lunghi pomeriggi di eccitazione.
translation: The extra life one gains by reading does not discriminate between great works of art and entertainment literature: don't let yourselves be blackmailed by those who tell you that one must read only important books. I have intense and beautiful memories even of books that were perhaps silly, but which fed long afternoons of excitement.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:34:06)
notes: Eco text read in the film (an actor's reading of an Eco essay on why reading lengthens life); the sentence 'Non fatevi ricattare…' is the line most reviews quote (giovanniguarino.net). Caption 'sciiti' = 'sciocchi'. Research placement: 'corridoio (bookcase A: feuilleton and comics)'.

text: Rimane quella grande maggioranza che non legge perché non ha curiosità intellettuali. Avere curiosità intellettuali vuol dire essere vivi, e guardi che c'è mica tanta gente viva al mondo.
translation: There remains that great majority who do not read because they have no intellectual curiosity. To have intellectual curiosity means to be alive, and mind you, there aren't that many people alive in the world.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:41:01)
notes: Archival interview; quoted on the Film Forum page as 'To be intellectually curious is to be alive. And believe me, a lot of people are not alive.'

text: Se dovessi raccontare la biblioteca di mio padre inizierei da qua: sono i feuilleton, i romanzi d'appendice dell'Ottocento che lui ha letto da ragazzo e che in parte ha letto anche a noi. E qui si trovano le immagini bellissime degli incisori del periodo, che lui poi ha utilizzato tantissimo soprattutto nei romanzi, Il cimitero di Praga. Infatti qui c'è un segnale. Si estende un po' tutta la letteratura francese lungo questa linea, e anche qua; mentre qui sotto, ad esempio, c'è la letteratura italiana, e se andiamo invece verso l'alto rimaniamo sempre nell'ambito della letteratura popolare e arriviamo fino ai fumetti, che però sono sempre temi interconnessi.
translation: If I had to tell the story of my father's library I would start from here: these are the feuilletons, the nineteenth-century serial novels that he read as a boy and that he partly read to us too. And here are the beautiful images by the engravers of the period, which he then used a great deal, especially in the novels, The Prague Cemetery. In fact there is a bookmark here. The whole of French literature more or less stretches along this line, and here too; while down here, for instance, is Italian literature, and if we go upwards instead we stay within popular literature and get as far as the comics, which are however always interconnected themes.
speaker: Carlotta Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:43:09)
notes: On-camera walk along the corridor: feuilletons at the centre, French literature along one line, Italian below, popular literature and comics on the top shelves. Matches CriticaLetteraria (comics on highest/lowest shelves) and Fedriga (Domani 2026). Research placement: 'corridoio (bookcase A)'.

text: Questa biblioteca di lavoro è sì organizzata per settori, ma non è organizzata alfabeticamente, ma piuttosto per sottosettori dove poi alcune cose venivano spostate. Insomma, lo sapeva quasi solo lui dove trovare i libri, perché era una cosa viva: non era un archivio, non era una biblioteca codificata nel senso classico, ma questi erano i libri più amati. Però lui era curioso di tantissime cose, anche delle cose più bislacche.
translation: This working library is indeed organised by sections, but it is not organised alphabetically, rather by sub-sections, within which things then got moved around. In short, almost only he knew where to find the books, because it was a living thing: it was not an archive, it was not a library codified in the classical sense, but these were the most loved books. Yet he was curious about a great many things, even the most bizarre ones.
speaker: Carlotta Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:44:09)
notes: Key statement on the arrangement principle of the working library. Il Bo Live attributes 'lo sapeva quasi solo lui dove erano' to Stefano Eco; in the film the voice is Carlotta's.

text: Sono tornato a casa e ho cominciato a buttar giù una lista di nomi di monaci, e poi ho scritto a un amico chimico come si può avvelenare una persona mentre legge un libro. Lui mi ha risposto, poi ho distrutto la lettera.
translation: I went home and started jotting down a list of monks' names, and then I wrote to a chemist friend asking how one can poison a person while he is reading a book. He answered me, then I destroyed the letter.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:48:33)
notes: Origin of The Name of the Rose told as a list; same anecdote in the Paris Review ('making a list of names of fictional medieval monks') and the Louisiana interview (M8IWTOFNlOc 00:03:05).

text: Questa biblioteca ha anche un suo profumo, un odore, e anche un suono, direi, perché quando ti muovi in quei corridoi pieni di libri tutto è più attutito. Io mi sento molto protetta lì in mezzo.
translation: This library also has its own perfume, a smell, and also a sound, I would say, because when you move through those corridors full of books everything is more muffled. I feel very protected in the middle of it.
speaker: Eco family member (female voice; probably Carlotta Eco — not identified by caption)
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:51:04)
notes: The Common Reader review misattributes this to Eco; the Italian is in the feminine ('protetta').

text: Ho cominciato negli anni Settanta a occuparmi della bugia. Nel mio Trattato di semiotica generale si dice che il segno è tutto ciò che può essere usato per mentire, una definizione che ha avuto qualche fortuna. Di lì l'interesse per il falso. […] Poi avevo scritto un saggio su come i falsi avevano influenzato la storia: molti documenti falsi hanno però provocato dei grandi avvenimenti storici, la donazione di Costantino, la lettera del Prete Gianni che ha spinto all'esplorazione prima dell'Asia e poi dell'Africa.
translation: I began in the 1970s to concern myself with the lie. In my Theory of Semiotics it is said that a sign is everything that can be used to lie, a definition that has enjoyed some success. From there came the interest in the fake. […] Then I had written an essay on how forgeries had influenced history: many forged documents have provoked great historical events, the Donation of Constantine, the letter of Prester John which drove the exploration first of Asia and then of Africa.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 01:02:23)
notes: The semiotic rationale for a library of 'books that lie'; Guardian 2011: 'From lies to forgeries the step is not so long, and I have written technical essays on the logic of forgeries and on the influence of forgeries on history.'

text: La lista mi ha sempre affascinato. Ha la lista qualche cosa a che vedere con la memoria? Ma sì, perché è un modo di raccogliere tutto quello che si sapeva a proposito di qualcosa senza essere obbligati ad organizzarlo. Il primo elenco comincia col catalogo delle navi nell'Iliade: Omero non riesce ad esprimere la grandezza, la forza, l'immensità dell'esercito acheo che sta sbarcando, e fa un elenco, un elenco delle navi.
translation: The list has always fascinated me. Does the list have something to do with memory? Well yes, because it is a way of gathering everything that was known about something without being obliged to organise it. The first list begins with the catalogue of ships in the Iliad: Homer cannot express the greatness, the strength, the immensity of the Achaean army that is landing, and he makes a list, a list of the ships.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. Sulla memoria. Una conversazione in tre parti' (video installation for the Venice Art Biennale, 2015), Italian auto-captions, part 3 (caption time 00:03:11)
notes: Lists as unorganised memory — the same argument as The Infinity of Lists (2009) and the Spiegel interview; caption 'AEO' = 'acheo'.

text: Noi, nella misura in cui possiamo dire "io", siamo la nostra memoria, cioè la memoria è l'anima. Se uno perde totalmente la memoria diventa un vegetale e non ha più l'anima. […] La memoria collettiva è l'identità collettiva. […] C'è un corrispettivo della memoria individuale che è la memoria vegetale della biblioteca: l'insieme delle biblioteche è l'insieme della memoria dell'umanità.
translation: We, insofar as we can say "I", are our memory, that is, memory is the soul. If someone totally loses his memory he becomes a vegetable and no longer has a soul. […] Collective memory is collective identity. […] There is a counterpart of individual memory, which is the vegetal memory of the library: the sum of all libraries is the sum of humanity's memory.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. Sulla memoria. Una conversazione in tre parti' (video installation for the Venice Art Biennale, 2015), Italian auto-captions, part 1 (caption times 00:00:43, 00:03:08, 00:03:25)
notes: Narration of the Biennale installation; the walk through the corridors starts around 00:04:54 (music only) after 'la biblioteca delle biblioteche' at 00:04:50.

text: Senza memoria non c'è anima. Per proiettarci sul futuro bisogna avere un'anima.
translation: Without memory there is no soul. To project ourselves onto the future we must have a soul.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. Sulla memoria. Una conversazione in tre parti' (video installation for the Venice Art Biennale, 2015), Italian auto-captions, part 2 (caption time 00:04:47)
notes: Preceded by 'siamo come l'atleta che per fare un balzo avanti deve fare sempre un passo indietro' (00:04:07).

text: I am a rare books collector too. And my collection concerns only fake books - books that say the contrary of... So, I don't have Galileo Galilei but I have Ptolemy because it was wrong about the movement of the Earth. All together in different places there should be about 50,000. Here, when I arrived 25 years ago there were 30,000, but since, many of them... I have no more time to count them, but I think there are 35,000. [Interviewer: Do you have time to read a lot?] Another provocative way to answer such a question is: I don't read - I write.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: 'Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating', Louisiana Channel (Louisiana Museum of Modern Art), interview by Tonny Vorm in Eco's Milan apartment, May 2015; English subtitles, 00:22:30–00:23:19
notes: Eco's last filmed statement of the numbers (30,000 at arrival in Piazza Castello c. 1990, c. 35,000 in 2015, c. 50,000 overall) and the 'I don't read, I write' quip.

text: It was while I was working on Foucault's Pendulum that I started receiving the money from the translation of The Name of the Rose. And I decided to use it to buy these books. […] I have always been obsessed—also in my role as a scholar—with the problem of fakes and forgeries. […] This collection of books is my way to try to understand falsification and lies. […] There are no books by Galileo in my collection, but Ptolemy is there. Because Galileo told the truth, while poor old Ptolemy was in error.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Patricia Guy, 'The Parasitic Press: Umberto Eco', Publishers Weekly, 23 October 2015 (interview in Eco's Milan apartment)
notes: Dates the start of the rare-book collection to the mid-1980s (Name of the Rose royalties); Eco also explains that 'semiologic, curiosity, lunatic, magic, and pneumatic' are 'the words used in antique catalogues to describe books that are about falsity and frauds'.

text: Sono un collezionista a soggetto e la mia raccolta si intitola Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa, magica et pneumatica (titolo derivato da alcuni manuali celebri come quello di Graesse). Cerco linguaggi strani, dalle lingue inventate all'alchimia, le mnemotecniche e le steganografie. In genere libri che dicano il falso, per cui ho Tolomeo ma non Galileo.
translation: I am a subject collector and my collection is titled Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa, magica et pneumatica (a title derived from some famous handbooks such as Graesse's). I look for strange languages, from invented languages to alchemy, mnemonics and steganographies. Generally books that say what is false, which is why I have Ptolemy but not Galileo.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, as quoted ('mi disse una volta Eco') in 'Il mondo di Eco in una stanza', Corriere del Ticino, 26 June 2022
notes: The newspaper prints the title as 'Biliotheca'; the collection's name is given here as Eco wrote it.

text: Il piacere di un bibliofilo è quello di compulsare cataloghi, di fare collazioni, di aggiornare continuamente le notizie su un libro. E naturalmente di sfogliare, rivedere le incisioni, toccare la carta che fa ancora crac crac sotto le dita, mentre gli e-books non reagiscono al tatto.
translation: A bibliophile's pleasure is to pore over catalogues, to collate, to keep updating the notes on a book. And naturally to leaf through, look again at the engravings, touch the paper that still goes crack crack under one's fingers, while e-books do not respond to the touch.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, from the essay 'Collazioni di un collezionista', as quoted in 'Il mondo di Eco in una stanza', Corriere del Ticino, 26 June 2022
notes: The same essay is the source of 'se per avere un libro non ha compiuto un sacrificio, non c'è piacere della conquista'.

text: my personal 'Bibliotheca Semiologica Curiosa, Lunatica, Magica et Pneumatica,' which has been a mainstay to me in the present endeavor.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Umberto Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language, trans. James Fentress (Oxford: Blackwell, 1995), acknowledgements, pp. 5–6
notes: Earliest printed use of the name found; Eco there says the passion for 'old books on imaginary, artificial, mad and occult languages' began with a copy of Wilkins's Essay towards a Real Character bought in 1983.

text: Macché comprati! Me li mandano, è per questo che non si può fermare…
translation: Bought, my foot! They send them to me, that's why it can't be stopped…
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Andrea Zanni, 'Intervista a Umberto Eco per WMI' (Wikimedia Italia), aubreymcfato.com, 13 May 2010 — visit to the Milan flat, 24 April 2010
notes: Answer to 'did you buy them all?'. Zanni's layout notes: 'La libreria nel lunghissimo corridoio è solo la narrativa, mentre la grande stanza contiene … sulla destra un'intera libreria di libri scritti da lui e tradotti in ogni lingua; sull'estrema destra vari scaffali di libri scritti su di lui; una parte centrale con la sezione dei cretini (Dumézil e Zolla…); il cimitero, una serie di foto di Eco con Montale, Moravia, Foucault'; rare-book room 'stanzino adibito, tutto in legno, un'enorme lente sul tavolo'.

text: As a scholar I am interested in the philosophy of language, semiotics, call it what you want, and one of the main features of the human language is the possibility of lying. A dog doesn't lie. When it barks, it means there is somebody outside. […] From lies to forgeries the step is not so long, and I have written technical essays on the logic of forgeries and on the influence of forgeries on history. The most famous and terrible of those forgeries is the Protocols.
speaker: Umberto Eco
source: Stephen Moss, 'Umberto Eco: "People are tired of simple things. They want to be challenged"', The Guardian, 27 November 2011
notes: Same article: 'His two libraries, at the homes he shares with his German-born wife Renate Ramge in Milan and Rimini, contain 50,000 books, including 1,200 rare titles' and 'He has called books "the corridors of the mind"'.

text: La stanza degli antichi fu da subito il rifugio di Umberto, senza telefono, senza computer, con gli spartiti e i suoi flauti, che suonava quasi ogni giorno. […] Umberto era fiero della rarità di molti dei suoi acquisti, e li mostrava ai familiari e ai pochi amici ammessi nella stanza con l'orgoglio e il sorriso del collezionista appassionato. […] Ai nipoti mostrava con divertimento gli animali, i mostri e le creature dai libri di Aldrovandi e Kircher, agli altri anche l'Atalanta fugiens colorata di Meyer [Maier], o la splendida composizione delle pagine della Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, stampata da Aldo Manuzio nel 1499.
translation: The room of the ancients was from the start Umberto's refuge, without telephone, without computer, with the scores and his flutes, which he played almost every day. […] Umberto was proud of the rarity of many of his purchases, and showed them to family and to the few friends admitted to the room with the pride and the smile of the passionate collector. […] To his grandchildren he showed with amusement the animals, monsters and creatures from the books of Aldrovandi and Kircher; to others also Maier's coloured Atalanta fugiens, or the splendid page composition of the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, printed by Aldus Manutius in 1499.
speaker: Renate Ramge, Carlotta Eco and Stefano Eco (joint statement)
source: ANSA, 'Lo studiolo di Umberto Eco alla Biblioteca Braidense apre per la prima volta al pubblico', 4 May 2022; also Fondazione Umberto Eco, 'Le biblioteche', and Rivista Studio, 8 May 2022
notes: Family description of the Stanza degli antichi, which the Braidense 'Studiolo Umberto Eco' (open since 5 May 2022) reproduces in size and atmosphere; the original room was elliptical, the Braidense one rectangular (Rivista Studio).

text: Lui voleva che i suoi libri rari rimanessero a Milano, e venissero in biblioteca. […] A casa sua, i libri rari erano privilegiati, e posizionati separatamente rispetto alla sua biblioteca moderna.
translation: He wanted his rare books to stay in Milan, and to come to the library. […] In his home the rare books were privileged, and placed separately from his modern library.
speaker: James M. Bradburne (director, Pinacoteca di Brera and Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense)
source: ANSA, 'Alla Braidense collezione di libri antichi di Umberto Eco', 1 February 2021
notes: Announcement of the state acquisition (1,200 editions, 36 incunabula, 380 volumes 16th–19th c.).

text: I volumi si trovano a Milano, nella casa disegnata appositamente per accoglierli, oltre trent'anni fa: un grande appartamento a forma di anello nei cui corridoi, dal pavimento appositamente rinforzato, vennero montate le librerie. Seguendo la strada tracciata dai lunghi scaffali a tutta altezza – letteratura italiana e straniera, poesia, narrativa popolare e di genere, feuilleton, fumetto, storia e critica letteraria, stampa, comunicazione e mass media, arte e iconologia – si giunge al grande studio di Umberto Eco, con biblioteche dalla complessa struttura a pettine e isola che ospitano volumi relativi a filosofia, scienza, storia, filologia, mnemotecniche, enigmistica, editoria, linguistica e semiotica, oltre ai libri di e su Eco.
translation: The volumes are in Milan, in the house designed expressly to receive them more than thirty years ago: a large ring-shaped apartment in whose corridors, on specially reinforced floors, the bookcases were mounted. Following the path traced by the long full-height shelves – Italian and foreign literature, poetry, popular and genre fiction, feuilleton, comics, literary history and criticism, the press, communication and mass media, art and iconology – one reaches Umberto Eco's large study, with bookcases of a complex comb-and-island structure holding volumes on philosophy, science, history, philology, mnemonics, puzzles, publishing, linguistics and semiotics, besides the books by and about Eco.
speaker: Fondazione Umberto Eco
source: Fondazione Umberto Eco, 'Le biblioteche' (fondazioneumbertoeco.org/lebiblioteche), Italian text; English version fetched directly
url: https://fondazioneumbertoeco.org/lebiblioteche (Italian wording as transcribed in /mnt/project-files/eco-sources/eco-sources.md §3; English page https://fondazioneumbertoeco.org/en/lebiblioteche verified)
notes: The institutional description of the route corridor -> study, and the key for the lettered bookcases (A corridor literatures and comics; B Jewish thought/magic/Kabbalah/Joyce; C books on books; D esotericism/encyclopedism/alchemy; E ancient art; F aesthetics/photography; G architecture/design/labyrinths; H contemporary art/theatre/music; I ancient and Christian philosophy; L medieval–modern philosophy; M continental philosophy and Eco; N translation/dictionaries/philosophy of science; O encyclopedias/semiotics; P text theory/semiotics/logic; Q Eco in 40 languages; R, S psychology/sociology/anthropology). Research placement: 'corridoio (A) -> studio (B–S)'.

text: Nella casa di Piazza Castello i libri erano disposti in orizzontale, su un lunghissimo corridoio. Questo consentiva di allineare le serie delle letterature – italiana, inglese, tedesca – e tutto confluiva nel centro di questo corridoio dove c'erano i feuilleton. […] Si diramavano tutta una serie di incroci, tra il colto e l'inclito. E questi percorsi cambiavano di continuo, a seconda delle sue ricerche.
translation: In the house in Piazza Castello the books were laid out horizontally, along a very long corridor. This made it possible to line up the series of the literatures – Italian, English, German – and everything converged at the centre of this corridor where the feuilletons were. […] A whole series of crossings branched off, between the learned and the popular. And these routes changed continually, according to his research.
speaker: Riccardo Fedriga (Università di Bologna; Fondazione Umberto Eco)
source: 'Umberto Eco, l'eredità dei libri e delle biblioteche: a Bologna una nuova casa per la sua collezione', Domani (editorialedomani.it), 2026, report of the event 'Le sfide di Domani' at Fondazione Feltrinelli, Milan
notes: Explains the corridor as a set of parallel literary time-lines meeting at the feuilleton section in the middle — the layout Bologna reproduced in its 'stanza delle letterature'. Research placement: 'corridoio (bookcase A)'.

text: Quando si parla dei libri di mio padre spesso si danno i numeri. Perché le biblioteche sono più d'una e il totale cambia a seconda di come li si conta. Possiamo dire che in totale sono circa 43mila. […] Mio padre non buttava via niente. Ed è stata questa la nostra rovina.
translation: When people talk about my father's books they often throw numbers around. Because the libraries are more than one and the total changes depending on how you count them. We can say that in total there are about 43 thousand. […] My father never threw anything away. And that was our ruin.
speaker: Carlotta Eco
source: Domani (editorialedomani.it), 2026, 'Le sfide di Domani' event at Fondazione Feltrinelli, Milan
notes: Family's reconciliation of the figures: c. 33,000 Milan + c. 11,000 Monte Cerignone = c. 44,000 working library (Fondazione), plus c. 1,300 rare books.

text: Eco catalogava per simpatia, per affinità intellettuale.
translation: Eco catalogued by sympathy, by intellectual affinity.
speaker: Carlotta Eco (as reported by CriticaLetteraria)
source: 'Un pomeriggio nella casa-biblioteca di Umberto Eco. Cronaca di un'esperienza mistica. O quasi', CriticaLetteraria, November 2022 (visit guided by Carlotta Eco and Mario Andreose)
notes: Reported phrase, not a full sentence in quotation marks. The article's room sequence: salotto (art books, encyclopaedias, atlases, the vetrina of current research) -> vestibolo (Joyce shelf; Kabbalah, mystery, magic, Templars, devil, alchemy) -> corridoio (the 'bosco narrativo': Italian and French authors at eye level from Dante to today; comics on the top and bottom shelves) -> studio (dictionaries behind the desk; one wall philosophy from the Presocratics; opposite side semiotics, linguistics, theory of literature; Eco's works in 60+ languages and books about him).

text: La cosa più straordinaria è che i libri conservano l'esatta disposizione originale voluta da Eco, rendendo le sale di questa biblioteca un vero e proprio laboratorio di idee che spazia dalla filosofia medievale ai fumetti classici di Linus.
translation: The most extraordinary thing is that the books keep the exact original arrangement Eco wanted, making the rooms of this library a real laboratory of ideas ranging from medieval philosophy to the classic comics of Linus.
speaker: Matteo Lepore (Mayor of Bologna)
source: Artribune, 'A Bologna inaugura la Biblioteca Eco: Palazzo Poggi accoglie oltre 30mila volumi appartenuti a Umberto Eco', July 2026
notes: Opening of the Biblioteca Eco, Palazzo Poggi (Piazza Puntoni 2), 1 July 2026: 32,000+ volumes in 10 thematic rooms, 600 linear metres of shelving; 'prima del trasferimento, la biblioteca è stata studiata e rilevata scaffale per scaffale'.

text: La mappa si sgroviglia nella stanza delle letterature. Quella italiana, francese, anglosassone, tedesca, mitteleuropea, slava, ispano-americana e tante altre ancora. Tutte queste sono disposte lungo linee temporali che possono essere lette in orizzontale, in senso diacronico. Se prendiamo la letteratura inglese, per esempio, si può iniziare a consultare dal ciclo arturiano a T.S. Eliot. […] Le linee del tempo, poi, giunti nell'Ottocento, si sviluppano in varie direzioni intersecandosi con i generi, come il giallo e la fantascienza, la letteratura popolare e il feuilleton.
translation: The map untangles itself in the room of the literatures. Italian, French, Anglo-Saxon, German, Central European, Slavic, Hispano-American and many more. All of these are laid out along time-lines that can be read horizontally, diachronically. If we take English literature, for instance, one can start consulting from the Arthurian cycle to T.S. Eliot. […] The time-lines, then, on reaching the nineteenth century, develop in various directions, intersecting with the genres, such as crime and science fiction, popular literature and the feuilleton.
speaker: Amalia Apicella (journalist, Il Resto del Carlino)
source: 'Inaugurata la Biblioteca Eco. Un viaggio di 32mila volumi nell'universo creato dal prof', Il Resto del Carlino (Bologna), 2 July 2026
notes: Description of how the Milan corridor time-lines were rebuilt in Bologna; the same article: 'La disposizione segue la regola del buon vicino… i volumi non seguono un ordine alfabetico o un rigido indice tematico, ma le relazioni interdisciplinari'. Research placement: 'corridoio (bookcase A) as rebuilt in Bologna'.
